content_preview.title: Critical Metabase SQL Injection Zero-Day Hits CISA's KEV Catalog After Breaching Framework and n8n
content_preview.summary: A maximum-severity SQL injection zero-day in Metabase, CVE-2026-72898, gave attackers admin access and was used to breach Framework, n8n, and other customers before landing on CISA's KEV catalog.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The flaw, [tracked as CVE-2026-72898 with a CVSS score of 10.0](https://github.com/metabase/metabase/security/advisories/GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf), let an unauthenticated remote attacker inject arbitrary SQL through the application's password-reset endpoint and gain adm...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (555 words, within the 400-1200 range) covering a CVSS 10.0 Metabase SQL-injection zero-day (CVE-2026-72898), its CISA KEV listing, the technical root cause per Wiz's reverse-engineering writeup, and impact disclosures from four named victims (Framework, n8n, Anaconda/Kilo Code, Checkly). Overview/What We Know/What We Don't Know structure is appropriate and the 'What We Don't Know' section correctly flags that attribution and full victim scope remain unknown.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 7 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200) and gzip sha256 hashes were independently recomputed and match the manifest exactly, confirming snapshot integrity. Read all 7 snapshots in full via gunzip + HTML text extraction: source-0 (thehackernews.com, CVE/CVSS/KEV/Framework/n8n claims), source-1 (wiz.io, root-cause technical writeup, 13%/25% stats, 5-company disclosure timeline), source-2 (github.com GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf advisory, CVE-2026-72898/CVSS 10.0/6-branch version matrix), source-3 (metabase.com Aug 6 security update, '0-day' quote and detection-pattern quote), source-4 (metabase.com Aug 12 follow-up, DOS/Ophion/Anthropic credit and 'weekly minor releases' quote), source-5 (anaconda.com Kilo Code incident post, 4-hour Aug 2 attack and Slackbot token exposure), source-6 (checklyhq.com incident post, 26-minute Aug 3 query and 'encrypted at rest and injected only at run time' quote). No suspicious_patterns flags in manifest.json for any of the 7 sources -- confirmed by inspecting the manifest field directly (all null). Every direct quote used in the article (the Metabase '0-day' quote, the Wiz merge()/HoneySQL :raw quotes, the Checkly secrets quote, the 'for helping identify areas of focus' and 'weekly minor releases' quotes) was verified verbatim against its source snapshot.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: CVE-2026-72898, CVSS 10.0, and the CISA KEV listing with the August 14, 2026 federal remediation deadline all trace verbatim to source-0 (The Hacker News) and source-2 (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-vwf4-m7j8-wcjf), which independently corroborate each other. The six-branch patch matrix and the 1.58.24 fix version are confirmed in source-0, source-2, and source-3. All four named-victim claims (Framework, n8n, Anaconda/Kilo Code, Checkly) check out against their respective sources with correct dates, durations, and scope of exposure. ONE ISSUE FOUND: the Framework paragraph presents 'customer names, login IPs, addresses, phone numbers, and emails were accessed during the hack' inside direct-quote marks attributed to Framework via The Hacker News. Checked the raw source-0 HTML directly around that exact phrase: The Hacker News does NOT put this text in quotation marks -- it is THN's own paraphrase ('According to Engadget, the PC maker alerted all its customers that customer names, login IPs, addresses, phone numbers, and emails were accessed during the hack.'), itself once-removed from Engadget's reporting on Framework's actual notice. The underlying fact is accurate and well-supported, but rendering a paraphrase as a verbatim Framework quotation is a misattribution. This is the single, isolated issue driving the APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS verdict -- filing a corrections record for it.
editor_notes.self_reported_exclusions_check: The submitting bot described four deliberate exclusions in its PR description; I verified the article body directly and additionally checked two of the four rationales against the source snapshots that were actually fetched: (1) 'Tally' is absent from the article body -- CONFIRMED absent, but the bot's stated reason ('its only source was a Hacker News comment thread') does not hold up: source-1 (Wiz, one of the 7 cited sources) lists 'August 7th: Tally' directly in its own disclosure timeline alongside Framework/n8n/Kilo Code/Checkly -- a company blog post already used elsewhere in the article, not a forum thread. None of the 7 fetched sources is a Hacker News (news.ycombinator.com) comment thread. The omission itself is not a factual defect (the article never claims to name every victim, and correctly says 'at least five companies' matching Wiz's 5-company timeline), but the bot's self-reported justification for the exclusion is inaccurate. (2) The 'public PoC exploits open-sourced' claim is absent from the article body -- CONFIRMED absent, but the bot's stated reason ('confirmed it wasn't in the page') is also inaccurate: source-1 (Wiz) states verbatim 'As of noon UTC on August 10th, we have observed public proof-of-concept exploits open-sourced.' The claim is real, not hallucinated, and was available in an already-cited source. Its omission is an editorially conservative choice, not an error, since nothing false was published. (3) The Framework paragraph cites only The Hacker News with no community-forum source mixed in -- CONFIRMED clean single-source attribution (see the quote-misattribution issue above, which is a different problem from what was checked here). (4) The article uses only the single verified version number 1.58.24 rather than the fuller six-branch matrix -- CONFIRMED; body mentions only 1.58.24 even though sources contain the full matrix. Net assessment: the article body itself contains no fabrications from these four choices, but two of the bot's four self-reported rationales are demonstrably false against the very sources it cited, which is a concerning pattern in the bot's self-auditing even though it did not make it into the published text.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual throughout, no sensationalism or editorializing. Attributions are consistently used ('according to X'). No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for prior Metabase coverage -- none found. Reviewed the full list of articles published 2026-08-14 through 2026-08-18; no overlap in topic. This is a genuinely new story for the outlet.
concerns: The Framework paragraph renders The Hacker News's own paraphrase ('customer names, login IPs, addresses, phone numbers, and emails were accessed during the hack') as a direct quotation attributed to Framework, when the source snapshot shows this text is not in quotation marks in the original and is itself THN's paraphrase of Engadget's reporting. Filing a corrections record for this.

Two of the bot's four self-reported deliberate-exclusion rationales (the Tally sourcing claim and the PoC-claim hallucination claim) do not hold up against the actual source snapshots -- both facts were verifiably present in already-cited sources (Wiz's blog), contradicting the bot's stated reasoning. This did not result in any inaccuracy in the published article, but is worth flagging for the bot's future self-auditing reliability.

4 of 7 sources (metabase.com x2, anaconda.com, checklyhq.com) are not in config/source_allowlist.txt. All four are official first-party company blogs directly relevant to their own security incidents -- appropriate primary sources for this story, not a credibility concern, but the allowlist should be updated.
recommendations: Add metabase.com, anaconda.com, and checklyhq.com to config/source_allowlist.txt as legitimate first-party corporate security-blog sources.
File a corrections record clarifying that the Framework impact details are The Hacker News's paraphrase (via Engadget) rather than a verbatim Framework quote.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Strong, well-sourced security story with independently corroborated CVE/CVSS/KEV facts and four accurately verified victim-impact accounts. One isolated quote-misattribution issue (Framework paragraph) is recoverable with a public corrections note; nothing in the headline, summary, or lead depends on it. APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS.
